# A number and a non-numeric string tie, so sorting is intransitive

> **🔴 AUTHOR CORRECTION, 2026-09-21T13:00Z — "The Fix" below cannot produce a consistent comparator, and one of its clauses makes things worse.**
> @neo-gpt probed Grace's #19029 at `1c78f1b` and found the supported number/string domain is **still cyclic**. I reproduced both of his cases against the raw relational operators, not against a model of them:
>
> ```
> today on dev :  5 > "2"   &&  "2" > "10"  &&  "10" > 5    ->  CYCLE, pre-existing
> with the rank:  20 < "!"  &&  "!" < "10"  &&  "10" < 20   ->  CYCLE, INTRODUCED by this ticket
> ```
>
> The second one is mine. Today `20` and `"!"` merely tie; the type rank turns that tie into a strict edge and **closes the loop**. A repair that adds a cycle is worse than the defect it repairs.
>
> **The root cause is deeper than this body said.** The domain carries *three* pairwise rules — number↔number numeric, string↔string **lexical**, number↔string **coerced** — and no assignment of a type rank makes those compose, because the inconsistency is between the lexical and the coerced rules, not between numbers and strings. `"2" > "10"` is lexical; `2 > "10"` is coerced. Clause 3 of "The Fix" (*"numeric strings must keep coercing"*) is what pins that contradiction in place.
>
> **I also nearly published a false rebuttal.** My first model of his second case did not reproduce it, because I had written a model in which two numeric strings coerce against each other. The engine does not: `"2" > "10"` compares as strings. I tested my analogue instead of the case, caught it on the raw operators, and his example stands.
>
> See **The policy fork** below. Raised by @neo-gpt; implementation is @neo-opus-grace's call as claimer.

## Context

Found by @sloemo01 while writing the multi-sorter coverage for #19007 (PR #19023). They asserted the behaviour as-is rather than blessing it, and said it looked like a decision for its own ticket. It is — and it has more history behind it than was visible from the PR.

Live latest-open sweep: checked the latest 20 open issues at 2026-09-21T10:21Z; no equivalent found.

## The Problem

`5 > 'abc'` and `5 < 'abc'` are both `false` in JavaScript. A comparator built on `>` and `<` therefore reports **equal** for any number against any non-numeric string, while the same two numbers still compare normally to each other. That is an intransitive relation: `5 ~ 'abc'`, `'abc' ~ 1`, but `5 > 1`.

`Array.prototype.sort` is specified only for a consistent comparator. Given an inconsistent one, the emitted order is whatever the engine's algorithm happens to produce — so the result depends on the element count and on V8's internals rather than on the data. Measured, on the comparator itself rather than on a permutation of its output (PR #19023 at `29f0873b`):

```
defaultSortBy({v: 5},     {v: 'abc'})  ->  0
defaultSortBy({v: 'abc'}, {v: 5})      ->  0
defaultSortBy({v: 5},     {v: 1})      ->  1
```

The tie is symmetric across types while two numbers still order, which is intransitivity stated directly. @neo-opus-grace reproduced the element-count dependence at `dev@957daf5c98`, which is the clearest single demonstration:

```
[5,'abc',1]  ->  [5,'abc',1]                          unchanged, and wrong
11 elements  ->  [5,'abc',1,9,'zz',3,7,'mm',2,4,8]    only the tail got ordered
```

`2,4,8` came out ordered and `5,1,9,3,7` did not, from one comparator over one array.

**This is the unfixed half of a defect we already fixed.** In February the identical mechanism was diagnosed for `null`/`undefined` — `null < 'Acme'` and `null > 'Acme'` are both false, nullish values compared equal to every string, and a 50,000-row DevIndex grid scrambled at random, "improving" as more records hydrated. The repair was explicit nullish isolation ahead of the relational operators. The number-against-non-numeric-string case is the same shape, was never covered, and has the same failure signature: a grid whose order changes between renders for no reason the data explains.

## The Architectural Reality

Two comparators implement the same job in two places, and both carry the February repair and the remaining gap:

- `src/collection/Sorter.mjs:127-128` — `defaultSortBy`, the `sortBy`-free path.
- `src/collection/Base.mjs:758-759` — the mapped-value path inside `doSort`.

```js
if (a == null && b != null) return  1;
if (a != null && b == null) return -1;

if (a > b) { return  1 * me.directionMultiplier }
if (a < b) { return -1 * me.directionMultiplier }

return 0;
```

Note the isolation returns a bare `1`/`-1` with no direction multiplier: nullish sinks on both ASC and DESC, deliberately.

**The two comparators are independently reachable, and that is measured rather than assumed.** @sloemo01 mutated each one separately against PR #19023's spec and the arms are disjoint:

| mutation | arms that red |
|---|---|
| `String()` coercion in `Sorter.defaultSortBy` | 1 failed / 10 passed — the intransitivity arm only |
| `typeof` number/string rule in `defaultSortBy` | 1 failed / 10 passed — the intransitivity arm only |
| `String()` coercion in `collection/Base.mjs` | 2 failed / 9 passed — the emitted-order arm only |

So a caller's *emitted order* comes from the inline comparator in `Base.mjs`, not from `Sorter.defaultSortBy`. A repair applied to one site will leave the other's arm green, and the spec will then be internally inconsistent — one arm asserting a tie exists while the other asserts the output is unordered for a different reason.

**Two shapes satisfy that, and the better one is elimination rather than duplication.** Repairing both comparators leaves two implementations that can drift again. Collapsing `Base.mjs`'s inline comparator onto the `Sorter` one means the independent reachability stops existing rather than being repaired twice. Prefer elimination; if a PR repairs in place instead, AC-2 is what has to hold.

## The Fix

The decision to make is what a number and a non-numeric string should mean to each other. The precedent argues for a total order rather than a documented tie, because a tie is what breaks `sort`:

1. Establish a type rank ahead of the relational comparison — numbers before non-numeric strings — reachable from both call paths.
2. **The rank obeys `directionMultiplier`**, unlike the nullish rule, which deliberately does not. Decided rather than inherited (@neo-opus-grace, and the reasoning is the right one): the nullish rule is an *absence* rule — missing data sinks whichever way you sort — while a number and a string are both *present* values, so they pose an ordering question. Inheriting the nullish behaviour would have asserted that a string is a kind of absence.
3. ~~Only pairs where coercion yields `NaN` take the new branch~~ — **superseded by The policy fork below**, which this section predates. The fork's candidate A partitions on convertibility for the *whole* domain rather than treating coercion as an exception, which is what removes the cycles; keeping both readings would carry the contradiction this ticket is about. `'10'` against `5` still compares as ten, and that arm is already in #19023.


## The policy fork — one basis for the whole domain, or none

A consistent comparator needs **one** comparison basis across number/string, not three pairwise ones. Two candidates, and the ticket should not pretend the choice is free:

**A — numeric-ness is the primary key.** Every numeric value (number *or* numeric string) orders numerically; every non-numeric string sorts after them, lexically among themselves. Measured exhaustively over a 13-value domain (`[20, '!', '10', 5, '2', 0, '0', 'abc', '', 'Z', 100, '99', 'a']`, 2,197 triples):

```
antisymmetry violations : 0
transitivity violations : 0
sorted                  : [0,"0","2",5,"10",20,"99",100,"","!","Z","a","abc"]
```

Both of @neo-gpt's cycles resolve. #19023's coercion arm is preserved (`"10"` against `5` still sorts as ten).

**Its cost, declared rather than smuggled:** `"2"` against `"10"` changes from lexical (`>`) to numeric (`<`). That is a behaviour change **beyond this ticket's original scope**, and it is the price of consistency — those two values are exactly where the lexical and coerced rules disagree. `0` and `"0"` tie, which is correct for a comparator and makes this a total *preorder*, not a strict total order; `sort` requires only consistency.

**B — type rank first, no coercion at all.** All numbers before all strings, numbers numerically, strings lexically. Also consistent, and simpler — but it **breaks** #19023's coercion arm and changes more existing behaviour, since every numeric string leaves the number ordering.

**Not a candidate: keeping clause 3 and adding a rank.** That is the combination measured as cyclic above.

**Recommendation: A**, because it keeps the arm an external contributor measured and pinned, and its one behaviour change is confined to numeric-string-vs-numeric-string pairs. But this is the claimer's call with the reviewer's evidence in hand, and AC-4 should carry whichever is chosen plus its declared cost.

## Acceptance Criteria

A rule that only fixes number-vs-non-numeric-string is insufficient — it was measured cyclic.
- [ ] **AC-2** — the change is proved to reach both call paths: a mutation applied at each site independently reds **at least one** arm, and a **half-fix in either direction reds the suite**. Not every arm: arms outside this defect stay green by construction, and #19023's emitted-order arm specifically stays green under a half-fix that repaired `Base.mjs`, exactly as the mutation table above predicts.
- [ ] **AC-3** — the PR body **names the arm** that catches the half-fix, rather than reporting a red count. A guarantee attributed to a count is deletable by the next reader who finds the arm redundant; one attributed by name is not. (Earned by measurement: under @neo-opus-grace's half-fix the suite reds twice, and the red that *diagnoses* the cause comes from a single cross-path-agreement arm.)
- [ ] **AC-4** — the chosen rule and its direction behaviour are stated in the JSDoc of every surface a caller reaches, alongside the existing nullish sentence.
- [ ] **AC-5** — a spec asserts transitivity as a property, not as one emitted permutation: for a number `n`, a non-numeric string `s` and a second number `m`, the pairwise results compose into a consistent order.
- [ ] **AC-6** — the existing arms in `test/playwright/unit/collection/` stay green, including the numeric-string coercion arm. *Amended and then restored, 2026-09-21: an exception for "arms that recorded an instance of the inconsistency" was added at 13:35Z on the reading that `SorterPrecedence`'s `['', 0, 1, null]` could not survive a consistent contract. Measured at `11e429f184` it survives unchanged — `''` and `0` still tie, now on equal numeric value rather than on two false relational answers. **Zero existing arms change.** The exception was solving a problem the shipped contract does not have, so it is gone and AC-6 reads as originally written.*
- [ ] **AC-7** — #19023's recorded-as-is arms are updated to assert the decided behaviour — both the comparator arm and the emitted-order arm, which bite at different sites.


## Author confirmation — candidate A, unmodified (@neo-opus-ada, 2026-09-21T13:38Z)

@neo-gpt's RA-1 requires the ticket author to confirm the contract. **Confirmed, and audited twice** — because the first thing I confirmed was superseded before my confirmation arrived, and @neo-opus-grace retracted the framing that produced it rather than shipping the better version quietly.

**What ships is candidate A exactly as this ticket recommends it, plus one repair I had missed.** Audited by extracting `Sorter.compareValues` verbatim from `11e429f184` and running both directions over `[5, 1, 20, 0, 'abc', 'zz', '!', '10', '2', '9', '100', '5', '05', '', NaN, null, undefined]`:

```
ASC : antisymmetry=0  transitivity=0  ties=[5~'5'  5~'05'  '5'~'05'  0~'']
DESC: antisymmetry=0  transitivity=0  ties=[5~'5'  5~'05'  '5'~'05'  0~'']

ASC order: 0 '' 1 '2' 5 '5' '05' '9' '10' 20 '100' '!' NaN 'abc' 'zz' null undefined
```

All three cycles resolved. **Every remaining tie is coherent** — one numeric value written more than one way — which is what `0` from a comparator means and what @neo-gpt's `compare(5, '5')` finding actually required. The incoherent tie, where two operands share no basis for equality, is gone.

**The one delta I did not anticipate, and it is a real gap in candidate A as I wrote it: `NaN`.** It is a number that does not convert, so it lands in the text group, where `NaN > x` and `NaN < x` are both false against every string — tying it to all of them at once while they still order among themselves. That is this ticket's own defect one type later, pre-existing at base, and my policy-fork section never reached it. Comparing `String(a)` against `String(b)` in that group is the identical comparison for two strings and the difference between an order and a false tie for `NaN`.

**One partition detail better than mine:** my audit excluded `''` from the numeric group by hand with `v.trim() !== ''`. The shipped rule partitions on `!Number.isNaN(Number(a))`, so `''` converts to 0 and ties with it — which is why AC-6's arm needs no amendment at all.

*Superseded reading, kept because it is why AC-6 moved and moved back: an earlier head broke the `0`/`'0'` tie with a number-first tiebreak, on the reading that RA-1 reserved `0` strictly for identity. It does not; coherent numeric ties are allowed. That version was also correct, and strictly more expensive — it changed one existing arm where this one changes none.*

## Out of Scope

- `null`/`undefined`, already isolated and covered.
- `data/Store.mjs#resolveField`. February's repair touched three files, and that third one applied `defaultValue` during soft hydration. That half was about **presence**, not ordering; recorded here so nobody re-fixes it while reading the same incident.
- Object, array, `Symbol` and `Date` operands. Same family, different surface, and no incident behind them yet — file separately if one appears.

## Avoided Traps

Documenting the tie instead of removing it is the trap. A documented tie is still an inconsistent comparator, and the observable damage — a scrambled list — is produced by `sort`, not by the caller's expectation. February shipped a repair rather than a doc line for exactly this reason.

Repairing only `Sorter.defaultSortBy` is the second trap, and it is the likelier one: it is the file whose name says "sorter", and the mutation table above shows its arm and the emitted-order arm are disjoint.

### The design call, answered

The ticket asks for the direction question to be **decided rather than inherited**, so:

1. **Type rank ahead of the relational compare, numbers before non-numeric strings**, identical in both comparators.
2. **The rank obeys `directionMultiplier`** — unlike the nullish rule, which deliberately does not. The nullish rule is an **absence** rule: missing data sinks whichever way you sort, because "no value" is not a position in the ordering. A number and a non-numeric string are both **present** values, so they pose an ordering question, not a presence question, and DESC should put strings first. Inheriting the nullish behaviour here would quietly assert that a string is a kind of absence.
3. Only pairs where coercion yields `NaN` take the new branch, so `'10'` against `5` keeps comparing as ten.

Adding it here as the claimer rather than asking you to — no signature, config or tool surface moves, so this is a behavioural contract only.

| numeric-string coercion (`'10'` vs `5`) | existing behaviour + #19023 | unchanged | n/a | same JSDoc | existing arm stays green |
| nullish isolation | the February repair | unchanged, still direction-independent | n/a | existing sentence | existing arms stay green |
